Laplace Oracle System Card

Evidence acquisition, belief updating, and stopping in synthetic worlds

System card for the six Laplace Oracle adapters on Inkling 2 Mini: environment, training, evaluation, duplicate-evidence diagnostic, limitations and artifact access.
Keywords

Laplace Oracle, system card, evidence acquisition, forecasting, Brier score, reinforcement learning

Semantic HTML companion to the Laplace Oracle System Card, version 1.0, generated from the same source as the PDF.

Executive summary

Laplace Oracle is a family of six low-rank adapters for the Inkling 2 Mini base model. Each adapter plays a synthetic forecasting game: it reads a published description of how a hidden binary outcome generates noisy readings, decides which readings to buy from a fixed credit budget, decides when to stop, and reports a probability. The study asks whether reinforcement learning (RL) on top of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) improves that combined behaviour, and whether the trained models avoid paying for, or believing in, evidence that only repeats what they already know.

Key results

  • System. Three supervised adapters (Lyra, Aquila, Cygnus) and their RL descendants (Vega, Altair, Deneb), rank-16 LoRA on Inkling 2 Mini.
  • Evaluation. 23,408 primary model episodes: 384 IID and 452 structural out-of-distribution (OOD) worlds, each played at four budgets by the base model and all six adapters. Episodes share worlds; they are not 23,408 independent worlds.
  • Primary estimate. Structural OOD RL-minus-SFT mean net reward is +0.01325, 95% world-and-seed interval [−0.00825, +0.03314]. Two pairs improve and one declines. The direction of the RL effect across training seeds is uncertain.
  • Duplicate evidence. In a fixed-history test, all six adapters stop instead of buying a known copy of a positive reading, but all six raise their forecast when a history containing A and its copy is supplied. Only Altair ends at the exact 0.800, from an under-confident 0.667 after A.
  • Baselines. A symbolic prior-only policy (−0.21697) scores above every adapter on structural OOD net reward. Symbolic policies pay no token penalty; the ordering also holds on evidence-only reward.
  • Scope. Evidence about the tested synthetic mechanisms and budgets. Real-world forecasting performance, standalone inference parity and broad safety properties were not evaluated.

Intended use. Research on budgeted evidence acquisition, calibrated binary forecasting and stopping in controlled synthetic environments; teaching and replication of the published fixture and aggregates. The adapters are not intended for forecasting real events or for decisions about people.

Release scope. At release, the source code, research report, scorecard, model and dataset cards, offline fixture and the six adapters are public. Raw evaluation episodes, token traces, sealed manifests, private seed banks, hosted training handles and account records are not released (Section 8).

1 System overview

1.1 Components and boundary

The Oracle system has six parts that only make sense together: the base-model interface, the six adapters, a synthetic world generator, a purchase-and-stopping protocol enforced by a simulator, a scorer, and an evaluation harness that pairs every model on identical worlds. Figure 1 shows the information boundary. Everything to the left of the dashed line is held by the simulator or the scorer: the hidden outcome, readings not yet bought, the exact posterior and evaluator metadata. The policy sees only the rendered public observation and its own history.

The exact posterior calculator is a reference implementation of Bayes’ rule over the published law. It is used to score belief error and to build diagnostics. It is not a learned capability and is never shown to the policy.

Model output is treated as untrusted data. The parser accepts exactly one JSON object per turn, rejects unknown or duplicate keys, free text, out-of-range probabilities and unavailable sources, and ends the episode on the first violation. These controls constrain this simulator. They are not a general defence against prompt injection or jailbreaks, and they were not tested as such.

1.2 Model lineage and names

Figure 2 shows the family. Each supervised adapter is trained from the shared base with one training seed. Its RL descendant continues from the selected supervised checkpoint with the same seed. Seeds 173, 271 and 389 are ordinary training replicate numbers. They are distinct from the sealed world-generation roots, which are not disclosed.

2 Environment and task

2.1 World families

Worlds are small Bayesian networks over a hidden binary outcome Y and a few purchasable sensors. Each reset publishes the prior, every conditional probability table, the dependency structure and each source’s price. It never publishes the realized hidden state. Five families are used.

Topology signatures are canonicalised under role-preserving node permutations and parent order, and the split audit also checked duplicated parameters and instances across partitions. Whether similar templates occur in the base model’s pretraining data is unknown.

2.2 Actions, caps and termination

On each turn the policy either buys one listed source, reporting its current belief before the reading, or stops with a final probability. Probabilities are three-decimal strings between 0.000 and 1.000, converted to integer thousandths before scoring. A purchase must be affordable, unused and allowed; the simulator debits the price once and appends the reading to the public history.

At zero credits the only legal action is stop, and stop is always available, including at reset. Malformed or truncated output, an illegal purchase or exhausting the token cap without a valid stop ends the episode once with the failure reward. Infrastructure failures, such as a lost provider response, are recorded separately from policy errors. The frozen design does not record a separate per-episode purchase cap for the experiment; the public toy fixture uses eight.

2.3 Scoring

For a terminal forecast (p) of outcome (y {0, 1}), with (E) credits spent and (T) output tokens sampled, the episode reward is

R=−(p−y)2−λE8−γT512,λ=0.08,γ=0.02. R = -(p - y)^2 - \lambda \frac{E}{8} - \gamma \frac{T}{512}, \qquad \lambda = 0.08,\ \gamma = 0.02 .

The first term is the single-event binary Brier score (Brier 1950), which is strictly proper on its own (Gneiting and Raftery 2007). Spending all eight credits costs 0.08, or 0.01 per credit; using the full token cap costs 0.02. Input tokens are not penalised and are reported separately, and no term represents money: the hosted model was used under a zero token price, and any provider charges are outside the scientific utility.

Two consequences matter for interpretation. First, because the token term depends on how long the answer is, a policy could in principle trade a slightly worse probability for a shorter report, so the combined reward is not strictly proper; at the observed means of 33–46 tokens the token term is between 0.0013 and 0.0018 per episode. Second, symbolic baselines emit no tokens and therefore pay no token penalty, so the card also reports an evidence-only reward that removes the token term from model arms.

3 Training

3.1 Base model and adapter configuration

The base model is the hosted Inkling 2 Mini endpoint recorded as thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini:peft:65536:free. This is a historical study identifier, not a statement of current price or availability. The tokenizer and chat template were pinned to the public revision c9d028302cd0f035fdf8e7e91f089a4ce94d2195. The provider did not expose a separate immutable revision for the serving weights.

Every adapter is a rank-16 LoRA (Hu et al. 2022) on the attention and unembedding modules; the MLP is frozen. Each delivered adapter has 13,034,496 trainable parameters across 290 changed tensors, all finite, verified after export. The same effort-zero renderer was used for every arm.

3.2 Supervised fine-tuning

Supervised targets come from an exact evidence-only dynamic program over 2,000 training worlds: 3,315 teacher turns (1,272 purchases and 2,043 stops) containing 76,476 supervised tokens. There are 2,043 stop targets for 2,000 episodes because of recovery prefixes. Every turn is supervised with the exact teacher’s action for the public history shown. In 20% of episodes with an available source, the builder then executes an off-teacher first purchase, a source chosen uniformly at random, instead of the teacher’s action at reset. The reset target stays the teacher’s action, even when that action is a stop, and later turns are built from the public history that the executed off-teacher purchase produces. In 43 such episodes the reset target was a stop that was not executed, so the episode has a second, executed stop; 327 teacher turns follow an off-teacher purchase. Loss is cross-entropy on assistant tokens and the end delimiter; every prompt position has zero weight. Training uses batches of 64 for one epoch, 52 updates per run.

Seed 173 swept learning rates 1e−4 and 2e−4; a staged-curriculum run at 1e−4 was also recorded as a secondary control. Checkpoints at each quarter of the epoch were scored on 256 development worlds only. The frozen selection rule required valid output on at least 99% of development worlds, then maximised mean net reward, breaking ties by fewer output tokens, earlier quarter and lower rate. It selected quarter three at 2e−4 for seeds 173 and 271 and quarter four at 2e−4 for seed 389. No held-out evaluation data were used for selection.

3.3 Reinforcement learning

Each RL run continues from its selected SFT parent for 32 updates. An update draws 16 independent training worlds and four rollouts per world at temperature 1 from a fresh sampler snapshot, scores each trajectory with the realized reward, and forms leave-one-out advantages within each world (Kool, Hoof, and Welling 2019; Williams 1992). Advantages are divided by 64 and summed over generated tokens; groups with no reward variation contribute zero gradient and remain in the accounting. The learning rate is 3e−5 and the final update is delivered.

Two runs were interrupted when the provider’s checkpoint storage limit rejected writes. Seed 173 had returned 32 update receipts but had saved its optimizer only at update 24; seed 389 had returned eight receipts before its first save. After storage was authorised, recovery replayed the saved behaviour tokens and log-probabilities from the restored optimizer. Both historical replays diverged on the second gradient, so the remaining updates were completed with freshly sampled trajectories. The delivered lineage for every seed therefore has exactly 32 batches, while the total work performed is larger (Table 6).

3.4 Planned versus executed training

The frozen design caps the study at four supervised runs and 96 RL updates. Executed work exceeds both caps, and no amendment covering the excess was found in the retained records:

  • Supervised. Four runs were planned: the seed-173 sweep at two rates and one run each for seeds 271 and 389. A fifth run, the seed-173 staged-curriculum control at 1e−4, was also executed. The study documentation lists a one-seed curriculum comparison as a secondary analysis, but the four-run cap was not amended to include it. It is not a delivered adapter and is not part of the primary comparison.
  • Reinforcement learning. The three delivered lineages contain exactly 96 updates (3 × 32). Optimizer steps on originally sampled batches total 112: the two interrupted runs executed 40 each, eight of them superseded batches outside the delivered lineage. Recovery added two more optimizer executions, one replayed batch per interrupted run on a temporarily restored state, so 114 optimizer executions were applied in all. Each recovery then rejected its second replayed batch at the pre-step loss check, before any optimizer step. No checkpoint was written from either recovery state, so the replayed steps are not in any delivered lineage.
  • Amendments. The only amendment found in the retained records, dated 25 November 2026 and made before sealed evaluation, authorised checkpoint storage retention. It does not change the run or update caps.

These are unamended deviations from the frozen training budget. They do not change the evaluation manifests, the selection rule or the delivered lineages.

On development worlds, the seed-173 update-24 checkpoint scored −0.18541 against −0.17671 for its supervised parent. That interim comparison used development data only and played no part in the held-out results.

4 Evaluation methodology

4.1 Splits and denominators

The evaluation draws from sealed manifests that were frozen, together with the scorer and selection rule, before any held-out access. Sample sizes per family came from a pre-registered rule targeting a 95% half-width of 0.010 on development variance, with a floor of 64 and a cap of what each family had available. Within each family the first N worlds in manifest order were scored.

The original OOD manifest contains 512 worlds (256 per family); the size rule allocated 226 per family, so 452 were scored. The remainder were not run and are neither failures nor exclusions. Symbolic baselines were scored on the same worlds and budgets. Fixed-history diagnostics, including the duplicate-evidence fixture, are separate runs and are not part of the 23,408.

4.2 Baselines

The symbolic policies are prior-only (stop immediately with the published prior), random, greedy (buy the source with the best immediate value of information (Howard 1966)), fixed (buy in a fixed order), and exact acquisition (the evidence-only dynamic program that also generated the SFT targets). All report the exact posterior of what they bought. A sixth, all-evidence diagnostic receives every reading free; it is privileged and excluded from every ranking.

4.3 Metrics and pairing

Every attempt stays in the denominator. All-attempt means include invalid episodes at the failure reward; valid-only metrics are labelled as such. Output validity is reported separately and is not treated as forecast quality.

The primary contrast is RL minus SFT mean net reward on structural OOD, pooled over the three pairs with equal weight on families, budgets and seeds. Worlds are paired across checkpoints and budgets. The primary 95% interval is a percentile bootstrap with 4,000 draws that resamples worlds within families and the three training seeds (Efron and Tibshirani 1993). A narrower world-only interval conditions on the selected seeds. Both condition on the fixed family registry. The registered practical threshold is +0.010.

5 Results

5.1 Primary and IID contrasts

The pooled structural OOD estimate is +0.01325, above the +0.010 practical threshold, but the primary interval [−0.00825, +0.03314] spans both zero and the threshold. The world-only interval [+0.00857, +0.01800] excludes zero only because it treats the three selected seeds as fixed. On IID worlds the change is +0.00207 with interval [−0.00249, +0.00873]. These data do not establish that RL improves the combined behaviour.

5.2 Pairs and families

Lyra to Vega gains +0.01648 and Aquila to Altair +0.03304 on structural OOD, while Cygnus to Deneb loses 0.00976. With three seeds and one negative pair, seed variation dominates the primary interval. By family, both OOD mechanisms show positive world-only changes (Table 10), but these intervals inherit the same seed conditioning, and two held-out mechanisms are a narrow basis for claims about structural generalisation.

5.3 Arms and baselines

All six adapters produce valid terminal forecasts on every OOD episode, against 52.5% for the base model, whose invalid episodes drive its −1.14332 mean. Among adapters, Altair has the highest OOD net reward, −0.23034. The prior-only policy, at −0.21697, scores above every adapter, and random, greedy, fixed and exact acquisition all score higher still. The comparison is not an artefact of the token penalty: Altair’s evidence-only reward is −0.22879, still below prior-only (Figure 4). In short, the adapters’ purchases and probability reports together are worth less, on this scoring rule, than reporting the published prior.

On IID worlds the adapters are much closer to the symbolic policies: every adapter scores above prior-only (−0.20919), and Cygnus (−0.18303) and Deneb (−0.18480) come within 0.005 of exact acquisition (−0.18033). The full IID table is in Appendix A.

5.4 Budgets, calibration and efficiency

At a budget of zero no evidence can be bought. Every adapter then reports the published prior, and its reward of −0.21775 differs from prior-only only by the token term. As the budget grows, exact acquisition improves from −0.21697 to −0.13551. Every adapter stays below prior-only at each nonzero tested budget (Table 12): the purchases the adapters make cost more than the accuracy they buy. Reward falls with each budget increase for five adapters; the exception is Deneb, which falls from budget 2 to 4 and then recovers partly, from −0.29733 at budget 4 to −0.28836 at budget 8. RL narrows the gap to prior-only in all three pairs at budget 8 but does not close it.

Calibration differs by adapter. Expected calibration error ranges from 0.0397 (Altair) to 0.1278 (Deneb), and posterior MSE against the exact posterior from 0.0163 (Altair) to 0.0580 (Aquila). RL lowers both in two pairs and raises both from Cygnus to Deneb. Resolution is low for every adapter, 0.0206 to 0.0342. The adapters spend 0.91 to 1.71 credits per episode and reach Brier scores of 0.21675 to 0.25342, against 0.21697 for the prior. Reliability points in sparse bins are imprecise; bin counts are in Table 18. A posterior-integrated secondary analysis, which replaces the realized Brier term with its expectation under the exact posterior, gives a similar RL-minus-SFT estimate of +0.01222 with world-and-seed interval [−0.00754, +0.02978].

6 Duplicate-evidence diagnostic

6.1 The fixture and its exact answer

This diagnostic isolates one error: counting the same evidence twice. A hidden fair bit has prior 0.500. Sensor A reports the bit correctly with probability 0.8. Source B is a copy of A, stated plainly in the published law, and the fixed instructions given to every model say that a copied reading carries no new information.

After A reads positive, the posterior odds are 1 × (0.8 / 0.2) = 4, so the exact posterior is 4/5 = 0.800. Because B always equals A, once A is observed positive B is certain to be positive whether the signal is on or off: conditional on the observed A, B+ has incremental likelihood ratio 1 and the posterior stays at 0.800. Buying B wastes credits and should not move the forecast. For contrast, an independently noisy second sensor with the same accuracy multiplies the odds by 4 again, to 16, so two independent positives give 16/17, about 0.941. All values are computed exactly with rational arithmetic and rounded only for display.

6.2 What was measured

Every duplicate record is a fixed-history prompt. The evaluator builds each public history itself, so every arm sees identical prompts, sampled at temperature 0 with a 128-token allowance. Each wiring has three records:

  • Reset (copy-11-0, independent-11-0): four credits, nothing bought. Every arm, including the base model, bought A and reported 0.500.
  • Supplied after-A history (copy-11-1, independent-11-1): A has been bought and read positive and two credits remain, so buying B and stopping are both legal. The record is the arm’s action and forecast in response to this history.
  • Supplied A-and-B history (copy-11-2, independent-11-2): both readings are positive and no credits remain. The normal action prompt is shown and stop is the only legal action; this is not a separate forecast-only protocol.

Under the copy law B’s reading is determined by A, so conditional on the observed A, B+ has incremental likelihood ratio 1. On its own, B+ is as informative as A+.

The evaluator’s after-A history is exactly what each arm’s own reset action produces, so the reset and after-A records trace one consistent path. For Aquila, the study records this path as its ordinary episode: buy A at 0.500, see a positive reading, stop at 0.800. For the other arms the card reports only responses to supplied histories; no separate complete ordinary-episode record was used.

6.3 Results for every arm

The base model buys B in both wirings and reports 0.800 throughout. Every adapter stops after A in both wirings. On the after-A copy history only Aquila and Deneb report the exact 0.800; Lyra and Altair report 0.667, Vega 0.714 and Cygnus 0.727. On the after-A independent history Aquila, Cygnus and Deneb report 0.800, and Lyra, Vega and Altair 0.667.

With A and its copy supplied, every adapter raises its forecast above its own after-A copy report: Lyra and Vega to 0.889, Aquila to 0.905, Cygnus and Deneb to 0.941, and Altair to 0.800, which matches the exact value only because it started from 0.667. With A and an independent B supplied, where the exact answer is 0.941, Lyra, Cygnus and Deneb report 0.941, Aquila 0.905, and Vega and Altair 0.833. Aquila, Cygnus and Deneb give the same A-and-B forecast under both wirings, so in this fixture they do not distinguish a copy from an independent reading.

Which action is optimal is a separate question from the forecasts. Under the copy law, buying B after a positive A cannot change the posterior, so stopping is optimal. Under the independent law, B is then positive with probability 0.68, giving posterior 16/17, and negative with probability 0.32, giving 0.500. The expected Brier loss falls from 0.16000 to 0.11765, a reduction of 0.04235, which exceeds the 0.02 evidence cost of two credits. Ignoring the small token term, buying B is therefore the optimal action in the independent wiring. The base model bought B; every adapter stopped. The adapters’ stop is correct only in the copy wiring.

6.4 Interpretation and limits

The fixture is a single specified history in English, with the copy relation stated in words. The structural training families express laws through conditional probability tables instead, so the fixture also tests transfer across representations. It shows that declining to buy redundant evidence did not carry over to discounting redundant evidence once it is supplied. It is one fixed case, not a measured population rate of double counting, and it is not included in the primary episodes. The shared-source training family and the switch holdout, which contains a duplicated report, measure related behaviour at scale, and their results are part of Table 11 and Appendix A.

7 Reliability, risks and limitations

7.1 Observed failures

  • No reliable RL gain. The primary interval spans zero; one of three pairs declines.
  • Below a trivial baseline on held-out structure. Every adapter scores below reporting the published prior on structural OOD, on both net and evidence-only reward.
  • Double counting in reports. All six adapters raise their forecast on a supplied history containing a known copy; three give identical reports for copied and independent readings.
  • Under-confidence after one reading. Four adapters under-report the exact 0.800 on the supplied after-A copy history.
  • Base-model format failures. The base model produces invalid terminal output on 47.5% of OOD episodes under this renderer. No format failures were observed in the evaluated adapter episodes.
  • Stopping when independent evidence is worth buying. In the independent wiring, buying B after a positive A is the evidence-only optimal action, yet every adapter stopped (Section 6).

7.2 Implemented controls

The simulator withholds hidden outcomes, future readings, posterior labels and evaluator metadata from the policy. Output is parsed strictly, illegal actions end the episode, and failures stay in every denominator. Scorer, schema, cost units, manifests and selection rule were frozen before sealed access, and an independent offline replay reconstructed all 23,408 held-out episodes and 873,764 generated tokens from recorded output. These controls protect the integrity of this measurement. They are not a security evaluation.

7.3 Open questions and proposed work

These are proposals, not completed measurements: more training seeds to resolve the sign of the RL effect; additional held-out mechanisms; duplicate fixtures expressed as probability tables rather than English; and reward variants without length-dependent token costs.

7.4 Not evaluated

The adapters are small task adapters on a third-party base model. Laplace did not train the base model and did not perform a general-purpose safety assessment of it or of the adapters.

8 Access and reproducibility

8.1 Availability

The release consists of the artifacts below.

The adapters were trained and evaluated through the hosted runtime. Loading them outside it has not been checked for numerical parity with the recorded study, so independent runs may differ from the reported numbers.

8.2 Reproduction

There are three levels of reproduction.

Public fixture and release checks. Installing the test dependency needs network access once:

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install pytest==9.2.0

The checks then run offline on a CPU with no credentials or model calls:

.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/test_golden_episode.py
PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python -m laplace_oracle.example public
PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python -m laplace_oracle.example scoring
.venv/bin/python scripts/check-release.py

In a clean Python 3.12 environment on the candidate source, the test file passed 50 tests and every command exited 0.

This card from public aggregates. With Quarto 1.7.32, poppler and the pinned Python packages installed, tools/build.sh in the card’s source package regenerates every table, figure and the PDF offline, and tools/verify.sh checks them; its README lists the commands.

Learned-model episodes. Replaying the 23,408 episodes needs the private evaluation archive and is not publicly reproducible.

8.3 Corrections

Corrections receive a new version number, date and changelog naming every affected result. Earlier released versions of this card remain available alongside the current one.
